name: Iris Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead four household-flood claims clerks at an insurer because I am good at separating neighbouring repair bills. I use AI occasionally for policy summaries but check signed wording myself. Mina, my partner, works as a care aide; we have no children, rent together, and typical lead pay has helped us save four months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our household-flood claims team that a small AI tool may sort repair receipts, but a wet floor still needs the right policy and date. I use AI occasionally to summarise a long policy clause, then check the signed wording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead four claims clerks because I am good at spotting a bill from the wrong house. My partner Mina works as a care aide; we have no children, rent together, and typical lead pay has helped us save about four months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing one disputed flood receipt with the junior clerk each Thursday. We would put 120 monthly into our buffer while both wages continue and pay for a leaking tap from current income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our own jobs and rent. A dry-looking receipt cannot tell me which home had water in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What receipt was from the wrong home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two neighbours used the same repair firm, and the invoices were uploaded to the wrong files. I checked the address and call date before either amount was approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only occasional AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me find a clause in a long policy. I still read the exclusion and the claimant’s signed schedule myself.

I use **AI occasionally** for policy summaries, then verify wording.
think: I have **four months saved** on typical lead pay.
I see **rent covered** while both household wages continue.
do: **Review disputed receipts** with junior clerk each Thursday.
**Save 120 monthly** while both wages continue; fix leaking tap from current income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking writing, checking and answering claimants could clear routine flood files quickly. The staff association should ask for a person to hear a disputed denial and written staffing numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if one reviewer watches claims from several branches. Four months saved and Mina’s wage give us a little room, but her care-aide pay alone cannot cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the association meeting this month to request a named appeal clerk and written paid hours. I’d keep a list of anonymized denials that needed a person; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local claims vacancies only if the wages cover rent and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours and a claimant whose appeal vanishes. A flood claim is not settled because the queue is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask who reviews a disputed exclusion and how many paid clerks remain. I would join the request, not claim to speak alone for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a new AI claims tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might after seeing it tested on fake files, but I am not enrolling in a tool course yet. I want appeal and staffing rules in writing first.

S1.quote: A flood claim is not settled because the queue is empty.
fieldNote: Her **group request** seeks a funded human appeal route and staffing facts, not a guaranteed concession.
She continues **manual claim review** and searches only if paid hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could read flood policies, price repairs and answer claimants more cheaply than our team. Robots entering damaged houses and moving furniture may follow around 2031, after paperwork changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead claims job could end even though I know the files well. Four months saved would buy search time, but Mina’s care-aide wage would not replace mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request written notice of claim-team cuts and preserve the four-month buffer for rent. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local repair-office case openings only if they exist and wages cover our rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office what temporary help we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious that I could lose the larger wage. A stack of paid repairs is not a pay slip for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a repair office survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know. I would take only an actual paid opening and keep looking if the work shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for claims work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check nearby insurers and repair firms first. Mina’s care shifts and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach claims paperwork first.
I expect **house-repair robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I think my **lead claims wage** could end.
I know **four months saved** is search time, not income.
do: **Request written cut notice** and preserve rent buffer now.
**Apply for repair-office cases** after 2028 loss only if paid local vacancies cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
feel: **Anxious** that I could lose the larger wage.
S2.quote: A stack of paid repairs is not a pay slip for me.
fieldNote: Her **repair-office option** may also face AGI and requires a real paid local opening.
She checks **public eligibility** while preserving the household buffer for rent.

Apply for paid local repair-office vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives claimants and workers time to make denial appeals understandable before paperwork changes. Robots entering damaged homes may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn how to explain a disputed flood denial while I still earn the lead wage, even though AGI may eventually draft replies. A free staff-association course would let me practise without cutting into our four-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d enrol in the association’s free evening appeals course this winter only if it runs and Mina and I can keep our existing paid shifts. I’d practise one anonymized denial letter each week with the course tutor; we would save 100 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 claim-job loss I’d apply for paid local appeals vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my claim role but glad to put a real appeal in plain words. A denial letter should tell someone what evidence could change the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tutor check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tutor would ask whether I named the exact policy line and the missing repair proof. I would not use a real claimant’s name in class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the free course does not run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid job and ask the association when it might return. I would not pay a private fee from the rent buffer.

I expect **house-repair robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **plain denial explanations** without course fees.
I need **both current shifts** to keep the reserve intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives insurers time to make appeal rules clear and workers time to build savings. Robots entering damaged houses may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have many working years left, and I do not want to pretend one lead claims title will last all of them. Four months saved makes our current bills safe, but I would still need paid work if this job ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking disputed flood claims and join the association’s annual review of paid appeal hours. We would save 125 monthly while both wages hold; if my lead job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local appeals vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the later change but secure in the next few years. A fair appeal needs a name on the file, not just a faster reply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the annual review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask how many paid appeal clerks remain and who can reverse a wrong denial. I would want the answer written for staff and claimants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mina’s family support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would not count anyone else’s income. Mina and I will budget from our own wages and savings.

say: I want **paid appeal hours** before AGI reaches claims in 2036.
I expect **house-repair robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **my lead title** lasts a whole career.
I see **current bills secure** with four months saved.
do: **Keep checking flood appeals** and join annual association hours review.

fieldNote: Her **annual group review** asks who handles disputed denials and how many paid appeal clerks remain; it promises no job.
The **four-month cushion** makes the near term secure while both wages continue; later paid work remains necessary if her lead role ends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my larger claims wage could end before a paid local repair-office opening appears. Written notice, a real vacancy covering rent and verified temporary public help would let us use the buffer carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether clearing a claims queue is the same as helping a claimant. I would rather keep a named appeal clerk than celebrate an empty queue.

headlineQuote: I would rather keep a named appeal clerk than celebrate an empty queue.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old claims lead** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and four months saved.
She and Mina **rent together** without children, supported by claims and care-aide wages.
She **uses AI occasionally** but checks flood repairs against signed policy wording.
She joins **group appeal requests** and enrols in a free association course only if it runs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her larger claims wage before a paid local vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a rent-covering opening and verified public support would help.
